title: United Airlines Announces New Empty Middle Seat Row
paragraphs: For many travelers, being stuck in the middle seat of a crowded economy cabin is one of the least enjoyable parts of flying. Now, United Airlines has announced a new option that guarantees passengers an empty seat beside them.

In July 2026, the American airline revealed that one row of Economy Plus seats on its new Airbus A321XLR aircraft will have no middle seat available for booking. Instead, passengers can book either the window seat or the aisle seat, while the space in between is covered by a fixed table that the two travelers share. According to reports, the table has a soft, leather-like surface and two built-in cup holders, providing both extra elbow room and somewhere to put drinks, devices or other belongings.

The option will be available on all 50 of the airline's A321XLR aircraft, and United has said it is exploring offering similar rows on other planes in the future. However, the airline has not yet announced the price, and tickets are not expected to go on sale until later in 2026. United says it expects to be "the only U.S. airline" to offer this kind of row.

The idea is not entirely new. In Europe, airlines such as Lufthansa, Air France and British Airways commonly use standard economy seats in their business class cabins on shorter flights, but block the middle seat to create a more premium product. In addition, travelers on some airlines have long been able to pay extra or buy an additional ticket to keep a neighboring seat empty.

The announcement is the latest in a series of efforts by United to offer more premium options. Earlier, the airline announced "Relax Rows," in which a row of three economy seats on some wider Boeing planes can be turned into a flat area for sleeping or lounging. Andrew Nocella, a senior executive at United, said, "We're investing nose-to-tail across our fleet."

Although some people believe airlines are focusing mainly on customers who spend a lot, United executives have rejected this idea, saying that their investments aim to improve the experience of every traveler.
